SCHOOL GARDEN · GARDEN THINGS

Garden Things

Age 2 YearsSubject Nature & TalkClass School GardenDuration 3–5 minutes

A garden is full of things with names: the tree at the gate, the watering can, the wheelbarrow, the bench where you sit. Twelve garden things, one big picture at a time.

Nothing to prepare and nothing to read. You say the name, your toddler points or wanders over — a moment on a card counts, and the real garden can wait for your next walk.

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the garden things cards together.

The twelve garden things print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the collection’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twelve, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each garden thing as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Name what it does

    Every garden thing has a job — the watering can pours, the boot splashes. Say the job with the name.

  3. 03

    Find them at home

    A watering can, gloves, a flowerpot — the house and the shed are full of these twins. One real find per card is plenty.

  4. 04

    Draw the tools

    Pick a favourite card and draw it on paper — or on its card page with the Write & Color layer.

Open the printable sheets ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

A name-it-as-you-go garden walk.

Take the names outside — or to a park, a balcony or a window box if a garden is far away.

Try one today

  • Water a plant together — pss-pss with the watering can or a cup.
  • Touch the tree trunk on your walk and say tree, big tree.
  • Sit on a bench and name three things you can see from it.
  • Spot a fence, a wheelie bin, a gate — garden words live on every street.
  • Dig in a sandpit or a pot of soil with a spoon — your own little shovel.

Real tools are grown-up tools: shovels and rakes and hoses stay in grown-up hands. Watching, naming and your own spoon-digging is the toddler version — with a grown-up close the whole time.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

Name the things you pass — tree, gate, bench. Everyday objects are the easiest words to practise.

Let them do the toddler version: water with a cup, dig with a spoon, push an invisible wheelbarrow.

Real tools stay in grown-up hands. Naming a shovel is plenty — touching it can wait for big-kid years.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Flower — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts with the word your toddler almost certainly has: flower. The card turns it into a game with rules — find one, name it, keep walking — and makes the whole street a garden.

    What is this?

    A flower is the bright, bloomy part of a plant. Flowers grow in gardens, window boxes, parks and even cracks in the pavement, in every colour you can name.

    What does it mean?

    Starting the set with a known word is deliberate: naming something familiar builds the confidence to name what is new. Every flower your toddler spots today is evidence that they already speak garden.

    What does the child need to know?

    Flowers grow almost everywhere once you start hunting — beds, boxes, buckets, cracks. We look at them, smell them gently, name them, and leave every one growing where the bees can find it.

    Why this matters

    A word your toddler owns is a door into the whole set: flower leads to petal, stem, colour and bee. Ownership also makes pointing compulsory — the card gives that pointing a name and a direction.

    What it teaches

    Rapid naming in the wild, colour words (flowers supply every colour), pointing precision, gentle-smell manners, and the quiet pride of a word used in the right place at the right moment.

    Words to learn

    flowerpetalsgrowbrightsmelllook

    Say this to your child

    “"A flower! Bright and bloomy — can you say flower? Flowers grow in gardens, in boxes, even in cracks in the wall. Let us find them today and say the word every time — flower, flower, flower! We look at them and smell them softly, and we leave them growing for the bees."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say flower, and ask your toddler to say it back — chances are they already can, so celebrate like it is breaking news.
    2. Find the petals with one finger, then the middle — the card is the day’s map of what a flower is made of.
    3. Play the pointing game at the window or on the walk: every flower spotted gets its name said out loud, all of them.
    4. Compare flowers out loud: this one is big, that one is tiny, this one is yellow — same word, many shapes.
    5. End with the gentle rule: flowers stay growing where the bees need them — we point and name, and the picking is for nobody today.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say flower and point at the bloom on the card together. Ask where its petals are, then look out of the nearest window and count how many real flowers you can spot from where you stand.

    Ask your child

    "Can you say flower?" "Where do flowers grow?" "Is that one big or little?" "Do we pick them, or point at them?" — answered with the word, a point and a firm little finger-wag at the picking question.

    What your child can say or do

    "Flower!" — from the buggy, at everything. Expect pavement cracks announced, window boxes admired, and the word applied generously to dandelions and weeds. All of it counts; all of it is the lesson working.

    Out in the real world

    Flowers are everywhere all year: tubs by doors, beds by car parks, weeds in walls. Each one is a chance to run the routine — spot it, name it, maybe sniff the air near it — and keep walking.

    Try it together

    Flower tally: pick a walk and count flowers out loud together — one, two, lots. Stop at the prettiest for a ten-second sniff, then let your toddler choose which flower was the champion of the day.

    Understanding check

    Listen on tomorrow’s walk before you say anything: an unprompted "flower!" at a patch of blooms means the word is working on its own — lesson complete.

    Parent tips

    Accept every flower claim, including wrong ones — the pointing matters more than the species today. Grow the game slowly: colour words and size words ride along free on every walk.

    Staying safe

    Flowerbeds are not for wading — stems snap, soil flies and bees work there. Sniffing happens in the air above a flower, never with your nose pressed in, and nothing in the garden goes in the mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Flower flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    Tree — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson goes to meet the real thing: your toddler touches bark, hugs a trunk, looks up a long way, and learns the one green giant that is always allowed to be touched.

    What is this?

    A tree is a tall plant with a woody trunk, branches and leaves. Trees live for years and years, and they change with the seasons — blossom, shade, falling leaves, bare branches, then round again.

    What does it mean?

    The tree is the set’s touch-me card: bark is safe, rough, wonderful under small palms. It is also the set’s clock — a tree your toddler meets every month is quietly teaching the year.

    What does the child need to know?

    Trees have a trunk you can touch, branches up high and leaves that come and go with the seasons. We may touch trunks and hug trees as much as we like; mushrooms and berries that grow near them stay look-only.

    Why this matters

    Touching a real tree wires the word in like no card can — rough, smooth, tickly, huge. And a tree your toddler owns as "their" tree becomes a measuring stick for the whole year: buds, shade, leaf-kicking, bare branches.

    What it teaches

    Sensory touch vocabulary (rough, smooth, bumpy), big-body awareness (how small am I next to it?), seasonal change tracking, hugging as gentle strength, and upward looking — a neck skill with a payoff.

    Words to learn

    treetrunkbarkleavestallseasons

    Say this to your child

    “"A tree! Big and tall with a woody trunk. Can you touch it? Bumpy, rough — trees love a gentle hand. Can you hug it? Can you look up, up, up to find the top? Trees give us shade and leaves and homes for birds — and we can touch this one as much as we like."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say tree, and hold your arms out wide — trees are the biggest growing things your toddler will touch all week.
    2. Ask where the trunk is and where the leaves are on the card — bottom and top, one find each.
    3. Take the card outside to the nearest tree: touch the trunk together and collect the words — bumpy? smooth? tickly? cold?
    4. Hug the trunk with both arms — squeeze as much as your reach allows — then tip your head back and hunt for where the tree ends.
    5. Close with the year promise: come back to this tree in every season and it will look different each time — that is the tree’s own story, told slowly.

    Look closer at the picture

    Hold your arms out like branches and say tree. Ask your toddler to find the trunk on the card — the strong bit at the bottom — then take the pointing outside to a real trunk you can actually touch.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the trunk?" "Is the bark bumpy or smooth?" "Can you hug the tree?" "Where does the tree stop, if you look up?" — answered with touch, a squeeze and a very long neck-craning point.

    What your child can say or do

    "Tree! Big one!" Expect bark-rubbing at every trunk, trees hugged on every walk, and demands to find "the top". Your toddler may appoint a favourite tree and greet it daily — keep the greeting going.

    Out in the real world

    Trees line every street, park and garden; a trunk is never more than a few minutes away. Each meeting is a rerun — touch, hug, look up — and each season gives the same tree a brand-new look.

    Try it together

    Tree meeting: visit one tree weekly and ask what has changed — leaves more, leaves fewer, blossom out, leaves gone. Take the same pose photo each time and let your toddler spot the differences first.

    Understanding check

    At the next trunk, watch the hands: they reach for the bark before you ask means the touch rule has bloomed into touch-joy. The arms-out wide on the word tree seals the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Let your toddler pick "their" tree and name it — ownership turns a plant into a friend. Keep the hug gentle and the looking-up long; the scale feeling is the part that lasts for years.

    Staying safe

    Tree hugging is safe; tree climbing is for later years and steadier legs. Watch what grows at the base — mushrooms and berries are look-only — and keep tiny hands away from anything furry or buzzing resting on the bark.

    This lesson pairs with the Tree flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Grass — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson sits down on the job: bare feet in the grass, one blade studied up close, the mown smell collected in one big sniff — the softest, tickliest card in the set.

    What is this?

    Grass is the soft green carpet that covers lawns, parks and fields. It grows millions of thin blades close together, and it smells amazing just after it has been mown.

    What does it mean?

    Grass is where toddlers already live — every picnic, every roll, every barefoot minute. The card gives that daily surface a name and turns a patch of green into something worth studying closely.

    What does the child need to know?

    Grass is made of millions of thin green blades, soft and tickly on bare toes. Freshly mown grass has a big smell worth one giant sniff — and we check for bees in the clover before any barefoot sitting.

    Why this matters

    Barefoot sensory play is developmental gold — texture, temperature, tickle — and grass is the safest wild surface there is. Naming the everyday thing under your feet teaches that every word in the world can be learned.

    What it teaches

    Barefoot sensory input, one-blade close observation (how thin is thin?), smell vocabulary, tiny-motor plucking with a grown-up pinch, and the body-satisfaction of lying down on purpose.

    Words to learn

    grassgreensoftticklybladesmell

    Say this to your child

    “"Grass! Soft and green and tickly. Can you feel it with your toes? Wiggle them! Grass is millions and millions of tiny blades — see how thin this one is? And when it is freshly cut, it smells wonderful — take a big sniff with me. Grass is the garden’s own carpet."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say grass, and stroke your own arm with spread fingers — grass feels soft like this, blade after blade.
    2. If there is a lawn, take off shoes and socks and stand on it together: wiggle your toes and say the words — soft, tickly, cool?
    3. Pick one blade (you pinch it, your toddler holds it) and look closely: this thin! One of millions!
    4. If you smell a fresh mown lawn anywhere this week, take the giant sniff together and name it: that is grass smelling amazing.
    5. End lying down: five seconds of grass-lounging, staring at the sky, before the tickle necessarily turns into rolling.

    Look closer at the picture

    Spread your fingers and stroke the air like brushing a lawn. Say grass, then ask your toddler to point at the green on the card — the carpet that holds the whole garden up.

    Ask your child

    "What are we standing on?" "Is the grass soft or spiky?" "Can you wiggle your toes in it?" "How many blades are there — one or millions?" — answered with toes, a touch and a loud "millions!".

    What your child can say or do

    "Tickly!" Expect barefoot requests at every lawn, blades handed to you as gifts, and the mown-smell sniff requested at every park. Sitting down mid-walk to wiggle toes is the lesson expressing itself.

    Out in the real world

    Grass is the most available nature in any town: lawns, parks, verges, football pitches. Every sit-down is a rerun — toes out, blades found, one big sniff if the mower has been recent.

    Try it together

    Toe race: on a safe lawn, walk a short line barefoot and describe the feeling out loud — cold, tickly, bumpy. Then sit and pull one blade each (grown-up pinch) and compare whose blade is longest.

    Understanding check

    At the next lawn, listen: "grass!" with shoes already coming off means the word and the feeling are bonded. A blade offered for you to hold completes it.

    Parent tips

    Keep a sit-upon or scarf in the buggy for damp lawns — the game should never be cancelled by morning dew. Say the sensory words as they happen; texture vocabulary grows one barefoot minute at a time.

    Staying safe

    Check any lawn before barefoot play — bees love clover, dogs leave surprises, and stones hide. Nothing green goes in the mouth, freshly cut grass can prick, and a quick hand-wash follows every rolling session.

    This lesson pairs with the Grass flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bush — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gets round: your toddler becomes a bush — big circle, then small — plays peek-a-boo behind the real ones, and learns that a chirping bush is a home with residents.

    What is this?

    A bush is a plant that is rounder and smaller than a tree, with leaves all the way from the ground up. Bushes make perfect hideouts for birds, hedgehogs and all sorts of small garden life.

    What does it mean?

    The bush is the set’s shape-and-hideout card: round is a shape your toddler can be, and a bush is a hiding place they can walk past every day. It is also the first home-lesson — some leafy balls have families inside.

    What does the child need to know?

    Bushes are round and leafy, and plenty of creatures live in them — especially in spring, when nests are built inside. If a leafy ball is chirping away, somebody is home in there: we look from a step away, and some bushes have prickles anyway.

    Why this matters

    Round-shape play plus hiding play is a two-lesson combination in one card. And the chirping-bush rule gives your toddler a reason to admire gardens quietly — the first brick of respecting wild space.

    What it teaches

    Body shaping (big round, small round), spatial words (behind, in, round), peek-a-boo with a nature twist, sound-awareness (is that bush chirping?), and gentle-distance manners.

    Words to learn

    bushroundleafyhidechirpinghome

    Say this to your child

    “"A bush! Round and leafy — like this. Can you make yourself round? Big and round... small and round! Bushes are hiding places: birds build nests inside, hedgehogs snuffle underneath. If a bush is chirping, someone is home — we peek quietly from the path and wish them a good day."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say bush, and make yourself as round as possible — arms curved into a big round hoop, then fold smaller and smaller until you are a tiny ball of bush.
    2. Ask where the leaves are on the card — everywhere! — then puff up round again, a whole-body bush with a toddler inside.
    3. Play bush peek-a-boo indoors: hide behind a cushion bush, pop out, giggle, hide again — then swap hider and finder.
    4. On the walk, find real bushes and peek around one edge together, quietly, to see who might be home.
    5. If you hear chirping from a leafy ball, whisper the news: a family lives in there — homes are watched from the path, not peeked into.

    Look closer at the picture

    Round your arms and say bush. Ask your toddler to find the leaves on the card — all over! — then be bushes together: one big round each, shrinking down to two small round ones on the rug.

    Ask your child

    "Is a bush round or square?" "Can you be a bush?" "Who hides inside bushes?" "What do we do if a bush is chirping?" — answered with a circle, a nest-story and a whisper: "listen quietly".

    What your child can say or do

    "Round and leafy!" Expect bush-shapes at random, peeking attempted behind every hedge, and chirping bushes reported like weather news. Somebody may insist the family car is a bush. Admire the roundness and move on.

    Out in the real world

    Bushes round every garden, park and car park — the most common shape in the landscape. Each leafy ball is a rerun: round body, peek at the edge, one listening moment, walk on.

    Try it together

    Bush and bird: one of you is the round bush (crouched, arms round), the other is the bird hopping close — then swap. Add a whispered "chirp chirp" from inside the bush for the full effect.

    Understanding check

    Pass a bush tomorrow and watch the feet: a pause and a listen means the home rule is rooted. A round shape on the word bush completes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Keep peeking to the edges of public bushes only — hedges by paths, never private gardens. The round-shape game doubles as a calm-up calmer: big round, small round, tiny round, still.

    Staying safe

    Some bushes carry prickles or irritating leaves, so peeping happens with eyes first and hands second, and every leaf stays unchewed. Standing bushes may host wasps — if buzzing starts, back away calmly, no swatting.

    This lesson pairs with the Bush flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    Garden Hose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is loud and wiggly: your toddler says whoosh like a hose, slithers a hose-snake across the rug, and learns the clean split — grown-ups hold the spray, toddlers stamp the puddles.

    What is this?

    A garden hose is a long flexible tube that carries water from the tap out to the garden. It unrolls, snakes across the grass, and sprays water wherever the grown-up points it.

    What does it mean?

    The hose is the loudest resident of the shed and the closest thing to a garden animal: it coils, it moves, it spits water. That snake-story makes it irresistible — and gives the safety rule a shape everyone remembers.

    What does the child need to know?

    The hose is a grown-up tool: the spray end can surprise and the nozzle is strong, so little hands never hold it. Toddler-sized watering happens with a cup — and the puddles a hose leaves behind are for stamping, not drinking.

    Why this matters

    A tool rule with a thrilling reason — the spray can surprise you! — lands better than any lecture. And the cup version hands your toddler a real water job they can own completely, which is the whole developmental point.

    What it teaches

    Sound play at full stretch (whoosh!), snake-slithering movement, tool-versus-toy sorting, water cause-and-effect, and the satisfaction of a job done with your own cup and your own two hands.

    Words to learn

    hosewaterwhooshspraysnakepuddle

    Say this to your child

    “"A garden hose! Whoosh — it is a long green snake slurping for the whole garden! It unrolls across the grass and sprays water. The spray end is a grown-up thing — strong and surprising — but your watering cup is all yours. And the puddles it leaves? Those are for stamping. Stamp, stamp, splat!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say garden hose, and make the long whoosh together — arms wiggling like water on the move.
    2. Tell the snake story: the hose is the garden’s green snake — it sleeps coiled in the shed and unrolls across the grass when it is drinking day.
    3. Slither a rope or scarf across the floor like a hose being unrolled, then coil it back up — snake home, shed shut.
    4. Say the rule plainly: the spray end is strong and surprising, so it stays in grown-up hands — your water job is the cup, and it is a good one.
    5. After the next real watering, stamp the puddles together — boots on, whoosh sounds optional but likely.

    Look closer at the picture

    Wiggle one arm like a wiggly snake and say garden hose. Ask your toddler to find the long tube on the card, then unroll an imaginary hose across the rug together — whoosh included.

    Ask your child

    "What does the hose say?" "What does the hose carry — water or milk?" "Who holds the spray end?" "What do we do with the puddles?" — answered with a whoosh, "water!", "grown-ups!" and a good solid stamp.

    What your child can say or do

    "Whoosh!" Expect hoses narrated on every garden visit, cup-watering claimed as a right, and puddles found on rainy days with stamping joy. The snake story may reappear at bath time with the shampoo bottle. Let it.

    Out in the real world

    Hoses unroll in gardens, allotments and car-wash forecourts all summer; sprinklers count too. Every watering session reruns the split — grown-up spray, toddler cup — and every puddle is a finale.

    Try it together

    Cup-watering crew: give your toddler a plastic cup and one thirsty plant — pss-pss at the soil, a little count of drinks, and a proud report at the end. Real job, real water, real pride.

    Understanding check

    At the next watering, listen for the split: "grown-up hose, my cup" means the rule is installed. A solid puddle-stamp with a whoosh attached completes the lesson entirely.

    Parent tips

    Keep a dedicated toddler cup by the back door so the watering job is always available. If the whoosh gets too loud indoors, whisper it — the wiggly whisper is somehow even funnier.

    Staying safe

    Hose spray can sting little faces and nozzles whip when water pressure arrives, so the spray end is 100% grown-up, always. Puddle-stamping needs grippy boots, and hose water — like all outdoor water — is never for drinking.

    This lesson pairs with the Garden Hose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Watering Can — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hands over a real job: your toddler fills the watering can, tips it slowly at the soil, counts the plants getting their drink, and owns the most respected chore in the garden.

    What is this?

    A watering can is a container with a spout and a handle, made for carrying water to plants. You fill it at the tap, carry it and tip it so the water sprinkles onto the soil.

    What does it mean?

    The watering can is the set’s responsibility card: a tool built at toddler scale. Fill, carry, tip, watch — the whole loop is theirs, and the plants visibly respond, which is responsibility with receipts.

    What does the child need to know?

    The can gets filled at the tap, carried with two hands and tipped low over the soil so the roots get the drink — pss-pss at the dirt, not at the leaves. A full can weighs a lot, so a lightly filled one — or just a cup — is the toddler-sized version, and spills are simply part of the job.

    Why this matters

    Real jobs at real scale are what toddler confidence grows in. Watering is visible work with a living result — the plant perks, the soil darkens — and the spout’s slow pour trains the careful hands that later carry everything else.

    What it teaches

    Two-handed carrying, slow controlled tipping, pour accuracy (soil, not leaves), early counting (one drink, two drinks), and job-completion pride — the seed of every chore that follows.

    Words to learn

    watering canpoursoilplantsdrinkgentle

    Say this to your child

    “"A watering can — the plants’ own teapot! Fill it up, carry it with both hands, and tip it gently: pss-pss at the soil, where the roots drink. Not at the leaves — soil is what plants sip. One drink... two drinks... There! The plants thank you. This is your special garden job."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say watering can, and mime the pour: tilt your hand slowly, sprinkle your fingers — pss-pss.
    2. Give your toddler a small can or a cup, fill it at the tap together — that is step one, and they can do it.
    3. Water one plant together: tip low, aim at the soil, watch it darken — the plant is drinking! Say so out loud.
    4. Count the drinks — one plant, two plants — and stop while the carrying is still fun, not freight.
    5. Close with the job title: this is your garden job now, the plants are counting on you, and every morning they get thirsty again.

    Look closer at the picture

    Tilt an invisible can and let your fingers sprinkle. Say watering can, then ask your toddler to find the spout on the card — the bit the water comes out of — and pour one pretend drink together.

    Ask your child

    "What do we put in the watering can?" "Where does the water go — on the soil or on the leaves?" "Can you carry it with one hand or two?" "Whose job is watering in our garden?" — answered with a pour, two hands and a very proud "mine!".

    What your child can say or do

    "Pss-pss!" Expect watering claimed daily at dawn, cans carried with maximum ceremony, and every houseplant guarded as personal responsibility. Spills will happen and should be cheered as practice, not scolded.

    Out in the real world

    Watering happens everywhere plants live — window boxes, balconies, allotments, grandma’s patio. Each session reruns the loop: fill, carry, tip, count, done — the most repeatable chore in the world.

    Try it together

    Plant drink shop: line up three cups of soil with seeds, and let your toddler serve each one a drink — one, two, three — then check every morning together for the first green speck of result.

    Understanding check

    Tomorrow morning, watch who remembers first: if the watering request arrives before yours does, the job has truly landed. A slow, low, soil-aimed pour is the skill ribbon.

    Parent tips

    Quarter-fill the can — weight is the difference between pride and frustration. Praise the aiming, not just the pouring, and let a wet patch on the path be the proof of work it honestly is.

    Staying safe

    Watering cans and slips go together: pours happen standing still, away from steps and slopes, on surfaces that can get wet. Spill water gets wiped before anyone skates, and the tap is turned off by the grown-up every time.

    This lesson pairs with the Watering Can flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Shovel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson digs: your toddler scoops, piles and pats with hands and spoons, watches the real shovel move mountains, and learns the tool deal that keeps everyone digging for years.

    What is this?

    A shovel is a big tool with a wide metal blade and a long handle, made for digging holes and moving soil. It is heavy, strong and firmly a grown-up tool.

    What does it mean?

    The shovel is the set’s tool-deal card: wanting to dig is right, wanting the sharp heavy tool is not. Your toddler gets the full digging experience — scoops, piles, treasure — through the tools that fit their hands.

    What does the child need to know?

    The shovel digs big holes and belongs to grown-ups — heavy, sharp-edged, not for little hands. The toddler deal is hands and spoons for you, shovel for me, and the two diggings meet in the middle of the biggest hole.

    Why this matters

    Tool rules with visible reasons (heavy! sharp! pointy!) are the easiest to keep. And hands-on digging is sensory-rich strength work — scooping, piling, patting — that needs no equipment and never gets old.

    What it teaches

    Hand and arm strength (scoop, pile, pat), tool-size sorting, soil science through the fingers, turn-taking on the big hole, and the patience of watching a grown-up do the heavy half of a shared job.

    Words to learn

    shoveldigsoilscoopholeheavy

    Say this to your child

    “"A shovel! Dig, dig, dig — it moves the soil and makes big holes. The shovel is a grown-up tool: heavy and strong. But look at your tools — hands and a spoon! Scoop, pile, pat... you are digging too. Grown-ups dig big, toddlers dig small, and both diggings end up in the same big hole."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say shovel, and mime one big dig — a long slow scoop through the air, finish with a tip and a pile.
    2. Ask what the shovel does — digs! — and where the soil goes when the shovel tips: into a pile, every time.
    3. Set up the toddler dig: a pot of soil or the sandpit, spoons and cups, and start scooping — pile, pat, pile.
    4. If a real shovel is about, watch the grown-up dig one big hole and compare holes afterwards: yours little, mine big, the same work.
    5. Close with the deal, hands dusted: spoons and hands for you, the shovel for me — and any treasure found belongs to the finder.

    Look closer at the picture

    Make one long scoop through the air and say shovel. Ask your toddler to find the big digging blade on the card, then start the real work: spoon in hand, pot of soil ready, scoop number one.

    Ask your child

    "What does a shovel do?" "Who digs with the shovel?" "What do you dig with?" "Where does the soil go when we scoop?" — answered with a dig-motion, "grown-ups!", "spoons!" and a pointing finger at the pile.

    What your child can say or do

    "Dig dig!" Expect soil mountains in the sandpit, spoons requisitioned from the kitchen drawer, and holes inspected for treasure daily. The deal may be recited back if the real shovel comes near: "grown-up tool!"

    Out in the real world

    Shovels appear in gardens, allotments, building sites and beaches — every big dig is a rerun of the deal. Beach spades and toy trowels are the toddler editions, and they count completely.

    Try it together

    Treasure dig: bury a few large, safe treasures (big pebbles, toy coins) in the sandpit and let your toddler dig them out by spoon — then bury them again for the next crew. Grown-up shovel strikes the mother lode, of course.

    Understanding check

    At the next real dig, watch the hands: they stay on the spoon while the eyes follow the shovel means the deal is holding. A "big hole, little hole, same work!" comparison is the graduation.

    Parent tips

    Join the digging yourself — a grown-up on hands and knees in the dirt is the best endorsement a garden can give. Rotate treasures so the dig never truly ends.

    Staying safe

    Real shovels are weighty, keen-edged and pointy — the grown-up keeps full custody, and no digging happens close enough for a swing to connect. Soil play means clean soil only, no mouths, and hands washed before anything reaches a face.

    This lesson pairs with the Shovel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Rake — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gathers: your toddler rakes the air like the real thing, drags leaves into piles with their own arms, and earns the grand prize of autumn — the jump-in, supervised and magnificent.

    What is this?

    A rake is a long-handled tool with a row of teeth at the end, made for pulling leaves into piles. You drag it towards you and the teeth gather everything in their way.

    What does it mean?

    The rake teaches gathering — a movement toddlers can rehearse with nothing but an arm. It also sets up the season’s great collaboration: the grown-up rakes, the toddler quality-checks, everybody jumps.

    What does the child need to know?

    A rake’s spiky row of teeth sweeps leaves up into heaps, and it is another grown-up tool — the metal ones stay in the shed. The arm version works anywhere, and the leaf pile’s true purpose is jumping, with a grown-up watching.

    Why this matters

    Raking the air is whole-arm coordination dressed as play, and the pile is the payoff that makes gathering feel worthwhile. The tool rule repeats what the shovel taught: big tools, grown-up hands.

    What it teaches

    Dragging and gathering arm movements, autumn awareness (leaves fall, then piles happen), jump-and-land control, tool-versus-arm sorting, and the deep joy of a job with a jump at the end.

    Words to learn

    rakeleavesteethpilegatherjump

    Say this to your child

    “"A rake! Scratch, scratch — its long teeth pull all the leaves into a big pile. Can you rake the air with me? Drag, drag, gather... The real rake is a grown-up tool, but your arm is a very good rake too. And when the pile is ready — you know what comes next. Jump!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say rake, and drag your arm along the floor — scratch, scratch — pulling an invisible pile towards you.
    2. Rake the air together, gathering make-believe leaves — then gather some real ones off the floor into one big heap.
    3. Point out the teeth on the card: a row of them, all working at once — that is how the rake gathers so much in one drag.
    4. Say the tool rule: the real rake belongs to grown-ups, the same as the shovel — your rake is your arm, and it works brilliantly.
    5. Promise the finale: when the grown-up rake makes a real pile in autumn, jumping in it is the toddler’s official job — one jump, two jumps!

    Look closer at the picture

    Drag one arm slowly across the rug and say rake. Ask your toddler to find the teeth on the card — the spiky row — then gather cushions into a pile with raking arms, scratch by scratch.

    Ask your child

    "What does the rake gather?" "How many teeth does a rake have — one or lots?" "Who uses the real rake?" "What do we do with the pile when it is ready?" — answered with a drag, "lots!", "grown-ups!" and a two-footed answer to the last one.

    What your child can say or do

    "Scratch scratch!" Expect air-raking in queues and kitchens, leaves herded into piles on every autumn walk, and jump-in requests at every pile seen. The arm-rake may be deployed to gather toys — accept gratefully.

    Out in the real world

    Rakes work lawns, parks and gutters all autumn, and leaf piles appear wherever trees do. Each pile is a rerun — rake arms, gather, admire — and the big jumps stay strictly in the grown-up-made piles.

    Try it together

    Leaf pile at home: scatter paper or fabric leaves, rake them together with arms into one heap, count the jumps over it, then rake again. Repeat until the pile or the toddler is fully autumn.

    Understanding check

    At the next leaf-fall, watch the arms: gathering motions aimed at a pile mean the rake has moved in. The tool rule said back unprompted — "grown-up rake!" — finishes the lesson.

    Parent tips

    Rake a jumping pile yourself this autumn and stand back — the delight is the lesson’s certificate. Keep the air-rake gentle around lamps and siblings; teeth are pretend but enthusiasm is real.

    Staying safe

    Real rakes have hard teeth and long handles that swing — grown-up custody, same as the shovel, and nobody walks behind a working rake. Jump-in piles get one pre-jump check from you: sticks, holes and hidden garden forks removed first.

    This lesson pairs with the Rake flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Wheelbarrow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hauls: your toddler pushes an invisible barrow across the room, drives a basket load of toys across the rug, and hears why the real one is a grown-up vehicle with a famous tipping habit.

    What is this?

    A wheelbarrow is a garden cart riding on a single wheel, steered by two long handles, with a wide open tub for hauling soil, leaves and tools around. You lift the handles and push, and the wheel rolls.

    What does it mean?

    The wheelbarrow is the set’s transport card — everything goes somewhere in it. Pushing, loading and delivering is a complete story arc a toddler can run with baskets and blocks, no garden required.

    What does the child need to know?

    The wheelbarrow carries heavy loads on one wheel, and a badly balanced load can tip it — something most adults discover the embarrassing way. Real ones are pushed by grown-ups; toddlers drive basket barrows and ride only with a grown-up steering.

    Why this matters

    Push-and-deliver play builds whole-body coordination and narrative play at once: load, drive, arrive, tip, repeat. And the tipping fact gives the real-tool rule a reason with a story attached.

    What it teaches

    Pushing strength and steering, loading and balancing play, transport vocabulary (load, deliver, tip), story-loop sequencing, and the gleeful physicality of being the cargo — a classic toddler role.

    Words to learn

    wheelbarrowwheelhandlesloadpushtip

    Say this to your child

    “"A wheelbarrow! One wheel, two handles — it is the garden’s lorry. Load it up — soil, leaves, everything — and push! Beep beep, coming through! If the load sits wrong, whoops, it tips. So the real barrow is for grown-ups to push, your basket is your barrow, and rides come with me on the handles."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say wheelbarrow, and take up the driving pose: palms flat, legs strolling — beep beep, load incoming!
    2. Push the invisible barrow across the room and tip a make-believe load of soil with a mighty heave — then do the return trip empty.
    3. Upgrade to real cargo: a basket of blocks is the load, the rug is the road — load it, push it to the other side, deliver, tip, repeat.
    4. Tell the tipping truth: if the load sits wrong, the barrow tips — which is why grown-ups steer the real one and your barrow is the basket.
    5. Finish as the cargo: if a real barrow is ever nearby, the toddler rides only with a grown-up on the handles — hands holding handles the whole slow trip.

    Look closer at the picture

    Drop into pushing position and say wheelbarrow with a beep beep. Ask your toddler to find the wheel on the card — just one! — then load, drive and deliver a pretend barrow-load across the room together.

    Ask your child

    "How many wheels does a wheelbarrow have?" "What does it carry?" "Who pushes the real one?" "What happens if the load sits wrong?" — answered with a push, "one wheel!" and a gleeful "it tips!".

    What your child can say or do

    "Beep beep — barrow coming!" Expect basket-barrows in constant service, siblings and teddies hauled as cargo, and tipping dramatised at every opportunity. Wheelbarrow may become the family name for any pushing game.

    Out in the real world

    Wheelbarrows work in gardens, allotments and building sites, and garden-centre displays count as sightseeing. Each real sighting is a rerun — name it, count the wheel, admire the load — at a respectful, non-tipping distance.

    Try it together

    Delivery run: mark a loading zone and a delivery point, and let your basket-barrow driver move everything from one to the other — blocks, balls, teddies — tipping each load with ceremony. Add a "fragile!" warning for the giggles.

    Understanding check

    At the next real barrow, watch the hands: they stay off the handles while the mouth says "one wheel!" means the rule and the word both landed. The beep beep is optional but traditional.

    Parent tips

    Keep basket loads light enough to steer — control is the skill, not weight. If your toddler begs for a real ride, do it slowly with their hands on the handles and yours over theirs: the safest seat in the garden.

    Staying safe

    Real wheelbarrows tip under wrong loads and roll on slopes, so pushing is grown-up work and rides happen only with a grown-up driving and hands held on the handles. No riding in tubs on hills, ever, and feet stay clear of the wheel.

    This lesson pairs with the Wheelbarrow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Plant Pot — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson plants something: your toddler learns the pot, tucks a seed into its soil bed, waters it gently and starts the morning check — the daily ritual that makes gardening magic observable.

    What is this?

    A plant pot is a little home for a plant, filled with soil. Pots come in every size, most have a small hole underneath to let extra water drip out, a single pot with a single seed is the whole idea of gardening, shrunk small.

    What does it mean?

    The pot makes growing visible and manageable: one seed, one home, one result. For a toddler it is the difference between hearing about plants and owning one — and the hole in the bottom is a genuine engineering lesson hiding in plain sight.

    What does the child need to know?

    A pot is a plant’s home with soil inside and a little hole underneath so extra water can escape — roots do not like sitting in puddles. The daily job is one gentle drink and one morning check: anything green yet?

    Why this matters

    Caring-for-something-daily is the longest game a two-year-old can play, and the seed sprouts on toddler timescales — days, not months. The waiting itself is the curriculum: check, water, wait, wonder.

    What it teaches

    Gentle watering control, daily ritual-building, patience in days-long stretches, observation skills (is anything different?), and cause-and-effect wonder — I watered it and it grew.

    Words to learn

    plant potseedsoilholewatergrow

    Say this to your child

    “"A plant pot — a cosy little house for a plant, full of soil. See the tiny hole underneath? Extra water drips out so the roots stay cosy, not soggy. Let us plant a seed in ours — tuck it in, water it gently, and every morning we check: anything green yet? Growing takes waiting, and we are very good at waiting."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say plant pot, and cup your hands around an invisible little home — that is what a pot is to a plant.
    2. Find the parts: the pot, the soil inside, and the secret hole underneath that lets the extra water out so roots never sit in puddles.
    3. Plant for real if you can: one cup, some soil, one big seed (a bean is fast), tucked in with one finger and a goodbye whisper.
    4. Water it gently together — a small cup, a slow pour — and put the pot somewhere bright where morning checks happen naturally.
    5. Start the ritual tonight: tomorrow morning, the first job is looking. Anything green yet? Not yet? Water, wait, wonder — same time tomorrow.

    Look closer at the picture

    Cup both hands like a little round home and say plant pot. Ask your toddler to find the pot on the card and the soil inside it, then pat an invisible seed gently into your own cupped hands.

    Ask your child

    "What lives in a plant pot?" "What is inside the pot — soil or sand?" "Why does the pot have a hole at the bottom?" "What do we do every morning?" — answered with a cupped pair of hands, a hole-hunt under an imaginary pot and a solemn "check for green".

    What your child can say or do

    "Green yet?" Expect dawn pot-checks in pyjamas, watering done with terrifying generosity, and the first sprout announced to the whole household at a shout. Beans deliver in roughly a week — plan the celebration.

    Out in the real world

    Pots live on windowsills, balconies, patios and shop fronts everywhere; garden centres are pot parades. Each pot your toddler passes is a rerun — name it, wonder what is growing inside, check your own on getting home.

    Try it together

    Pot parade: line up three cups with different seeds — bean, sunflower, cress — and let your toddler be head of morning checks: water, look, report. Cress sprouts in days and can be tasted on toast at the finish line.

    Understanding check

    The morning check arriving unprompted is the certificate — especially before you have had tea. A gentle pour that lands in the soil, not the ceiling, is the skill ribbon on top.

    Parent tips

    Beans and cress are the speed champions — pick fast seeds for short patience. Photograph the pot daily beside your toddler and let them spot the change: the sprout they find themselves is worth ten they were shown.

    Staying safe

    Soil is for seeds, not snacking, and pots are heavy and breakable — they sit on sturdy tables and shelves, never wobbling at edges. Watering stays small-scale near electricity-free windowsills, and any plant that sprouts stays unchewed until a grown-up says it is a tasteable one.

    This lesson pairs with the Plant Pot flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Fence — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson walks the edge: your toddler traces the boundary post by post, counts what passes, peeks through a gap to the world beyond, and learns the two fence rules.

    What is this?

    A fence is the line that goes all the way around a garden, made of posts and panels or wire. It marks where the garden ends, keeps balls in and shows everyone exactly where the boundary runs.

    What does it mean?

    The fence is the set’s boundary card — the first map your toddler can walk with their feet. Following it round teaches where home ends and the world begins, one post at a time.

    What does the child need to know?

    The fence runs the whole way round, and every post holds a piece of it. The rules: fingers stay out of gaps (they pinch), and gates open with a grown-up’s help — the fence guards the garden, and the grown-up guards the gate.

    Why this matters

    Boundary-walking is orientation, counting and safety in one loop. And the peek-through turns a barrier into a window — the world next door becomes a curiosity rather than a mystery, from a perfectly safe side.

    What it teaches

    Boundary awareness (where does our garden stop?), early counting on posts, gap-and-pinch safety logic, spatial words (around, through, over), and neighbourly hello-practice.

    Words to learn

    fencepostsaroundgapgateboundary

    Say this to your child

    “"A fence! It wraps right around the garden, edge to edge — post, panel, post, panel. Let us walk it and tally the posts as we pass: one, then two, then more... Look through this gap — what can you see next door? And our fence rules: fingers stay out of the gaps, and gates only open with me."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say fence, and trace a big rectangle in the air with one finger — around and around, the garden’s outline.
    2. Ask what the fence does — it goes all the way around! — then count the posts you can see on the card: one, two, three...
    3. Walk the real boundary at home or the park: follow the fence line the whole way round, counting posts as you pass them.
    4. Stop at a gap or a knot-hole and peek through together — what is on the other side? Trees? A dog? The world next door?
    5. Close with the two rules, hands demonstrated: fingers never in gaps, and gates open only when a grown-up does the opening.

    Look closer at the picture

    Draw a big fence line in the air and say fence. Ask your toddler to find the posts on the card, count the ones you can see together, then walk your own boundary at the first chance — post by post.

    Ask your child

    "What goes all the way around the garden?" "How many posts can you count?" "What is on the other side of the fence?" "Do our fingers go in the gaps, or stay out?" — answered with a count, a peek and fingers held up safe and sound.

    What your child can say or do

    "One two three!" Expect boundary walks demanded at every garden, posts counted on every railing, and hellos called over fences to dogs, cats and startled neighbours. Gate-opening will be reported to you for approval — take the promotion.

    Out in the real world

    Fences edge every garden, park, school and pitch; railings count too. Each boundary is a walkable map — follow it round, count, peek, and finish with a wave over the top to whoever is next door.

    Try it together

    Post count: walk any railing or fence and count posts aloud together — restart whenever you like, the counting matters more than the total. Finish with a proper over-the-fence hello to something: tree, dog, cloud.

    Understanding check

    At the next gate, watch the hands: they wait for yours means the gate rule is home. A fence line walked all the way round without shortcutting is the diploma.

    Parent tips

    Count posts loosely — "one, two, lots" is a fine total at two. If your fence has a favourite gap, make the peek a daily weather report: what can we see through the hole today?

    Staying safe

    Gaps between boards and wire can pinch or trap small fingers — hands stay flat on posts, not inside holes, and that includes railings. Gates open with a grown-up only, driveways and pools behind fences stay strictly supervised, and nobody squeezes through, ever.

    This lesson pairs with the Fence flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Garden Bench — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson sits down: your toddler learns the bench as the garden’s finishing line — the place where adventures end, snacks happen and the view gets named out loud, three things at a time.

    What is this?

    A garden bench is a long outdoor seat, usually wooden, where people sit to rest, eat and look at the garden. Every good garden has one, and every good garden visit ends on it.

    What does it mean?

    The bench gives the garden a shape: adventure, then rest. Naming the sit-down place teaches your toddler that outings have endings — and that the ending is a treat, not a punishment.

    What does the child need to know?

    The bench is where the garden sits down: snacks, stories and big looks happen there. Wooden seats hold the morning damp, so a grown-up hand checks first — then up you climb, and name what you can see.

    Why this matters

    A named rest spot builds the outing rhythm toddlers thrive on: go, go, go, then sit and say. Naming three things from the bench is observation, memory and language practice disguised as a snack break.

    What it teaches

    Sitting still with a purpose, observation and naming from a fixed viewpoint, snack-and-story routines, damp-or-dry checking as a life skill, and the calm pride of a completed adventure.

    Words to learn

    benchsitrestviewsnackstory

    Say this to your child

    “"The garden bench — rest stop! This is the garden’s own sitting spot: snack seat, story seat, the finish line of every trip out here. Climb up, wriggle in... now spot three things from up there — maybe a tree, maybe a bird, maybe a cloud. Wonderful looking! Every garden trip ends sitting together, right here."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say garden bench, and sit down on the floor cross-legged — the bench pose, indoors edition.
    2. Tell the bench story: it is where the garden rests — snack seat, story seat, the place where every garden trip properly ends.
    3. Play bench at home: sit together and each pick out three things in sight — a plant, a light, a teddy — then swap turns.
    4. At a real bench, the grown-up hand checks for damp first, then up you climb — sit, wiggle in, and start the naming.
    5. Close every garden visit the same way: bench, snack, three things named, story — the garden is officially finished, and the finish line is lovely.

    Look closer at the picture

    Sit down cross-legged where you are and say garden bench. Ask your toddler to find the long seat on the card, then name three things in this room, bench-style — rest included.

    Ask your child

    "Where do we sit in the garden?" "What happens on the bench?" "Can you pick out three things in sight?" "Who checks if the bench is dry?" — answered with a sit, a snack claim and three surprising nominees for the naming.

    What your child can say or do

    "Bench time!" Expect bench rest-stops demanded at every park, three-things naming attempted from car seats and high chairs, and snacks solemnly relocated to the nearest seat. The finish-line feeling is the lesson working.

    Out in the real world

    Benches sit in gardens, parks, bus stops and woodland corners everywhere — free resting, supplied by councils. Each one is a rerun: check, climb, name, snack, story — the most portable routine in the set.

    Try it together

    Three-things game: from any seat, pick out three things in view, then swap — your toddler names three for you. Vary it: three green things, three tiny things, three things that would fit in a pocket.

    Understanding check

    At the next park bench, listen: "bench!" with climbing intentions means the finishing line is installed. Three named things without prompting is the full certificate — with snack.

    Parent tips

    End every outing on a seat, even a step or a wall — the routine matters more than the furniture. Keep the naming light; two things and a giggle is a passing grade at two.

    Staying safe

    A grown-up hand checks any outdoor seat for damp, wet leaves and uninvited wildlife before little bottoms land. Benches mean sitting, not standing or climbing on backs — and snacks eaten outside need the hand-wash that follows every garden session.

    This lesson pairs with the Garden Bench flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).
